claims.text: High-entropy alloy nanoparticles containing five or more metals in near-equal ratios can initially form a homogeneous, single-phase solid solution.
The balance between configurational entropy and element-specific mixing enthalpies governs retention of the solid solution from 473 to 1923 K.
Dominance of configurational entropy over local enthalpic interactions causes nanoparticles to retain a homogeneous crystalline solid solution.
Low differences among the relevant mixing enthalpies favor retention of a homogeneous solid solution.
Large mixing-enthalpy deviations for particular metal pairs drive local phase separation and/or surface segregation during heating.
Replacing one baseline constituent with a metal having substantially higher positive mixing enthalpy with the remaining constituents increases the thermodynamic tendency toward demixing.
Local atomic-scale mixing and elemental segregation mediate structural and chemical stability.
At elevated temperature, phase stability is determined by competition between configurational-entropy stabilization and unfavorable metal-metal mixing enthalpies.
When entropic stabilization dominates, the single-phase structure persists.
When local enthalpic imbalances dominate, atomic rearrangements produce phase segregation or surface enrichment.
The baseline nanoparticles will remain single-phase throughout 473–1923 K.
Nanoparticles containing the substituted high-positive-mixing-enthalpy metal will exhibit more phase separation or surface segregation at elevated temperature than the baseline nanoparticles.
An inert atmosphere or vacuum isolates the proposed thermodynamic effects from oxidation and other environmental surface reactions.
Holding at selected temperatures for 1–5 hours is sufficient to permit potential phase evolution.
The mixing-enthalpy threshold for phase separation can depend on nanoparticle size and kinetic effects.
Nanoparticle surface phenomena may affect stability in ways not captured by bulk thermodynamics alone.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis says configurational entropy must dominate 'local negative enthalpic interactions,' implying those negative interactions oppose stability, whereas the intervention and mechanism identify higher positive or otherwise unfavorable mixing enthalpy as the driving force for demixing. The sign convention and identity of the competing enthalpic term are therefore internally inconsistent.
